source_lines.46: 1.1 Every right coset of $W_P$ has a minimal-length representative $w$; minimality gives $w(P)\subset R_L^+$, since otherwise right multiplication by a corresponding simple reflection decreases its inversion number. Such a $w$ sends all positive subsystem roots to positive roots. Along a reduced word for $v\in W_P$, inversion numbers therefore increase at each step of $wv$, giving $\ell(wv)=\ell(w)+\ell(v)$. Conversely this equality shows $w$ is the unique minimum in its coset: if $u=wv$ were another minimum its length would be $\ell(w)+\ell(v)$, forcing $v=1$. Thus $W^P$ is exactly this set of representatives. Applying [F1] to finite products and the cross-relations shows $H_P$ has basis $N_v\theta_\ell$ for $v\in W_P$, $\ell\in L$: these elements span the subalgebra because cross-relations and finite Hecke multiplication keep all finite Weyl indices in $W_P$, and are independent as a subset of the PBW basis of $H$. The length-additive factorization $N_{wv}=N_wN_v$ now proves $H=\bigoplus_{w\in W^P}N_wH_P$. Tensoring gives $I_P(V)=\bigoplus_{w\in W^P}N_w\otimes V$, including the injected identity summand, which is $H_P$-stable. [F1, F2, algebra]
source_lines.48: 2.1 Repeatedly move $f\in A$ through a reduced word for $N_w$ using [F1]. The leading term is $N_w w^{-1}(f)$; each correction omits at least one generator, so after finite Hecke multiplication it is a linear combination of $N_vg_v$ with $\ell(v)<\ell(w)$ and $g_v\in A$. Factoring each $v=up$ with $u\in W^P$, $p\in W_P$, gives $\ell(u)\le\ell(v)<\ell(w)$. The subspaces of $I_P(V)$ spanned by summands with representative length at most $k$ are therefore $A$-stable. Their successive quotients are direct sums indexed by the representatives of length $k$, with $f$ acting on the $w$-summand as $w^{-1}(f)$ on $V$. Commuting invertible operators $\theta_\ell$ can be simultaneously decomposed into generalized eigenspaces: take one lattice basis, split into generalized eigenspaces of the first operator, and successively split each stable summand for the remaining finitely many operators. In an invariant-subspace exact sequence the generalized $t$-weight spaces form an exact sequence, since their projections are polynomials in these commuting operators (finite-dimensional polynomial interpolation). This proves the multiset formula, including multiplicities and exactness under submodules and quotients. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

Its inverse scans $i=n,n-1,\ldots,1$: find the unique component whose recording tableau contains $i$, delete that recording corner, and reverse-row-delete the corresponding box of its insertion tableau to recover $\sigma(i)$; the component is $\kappa_i$. source_lines.40: 1.1 For each color $c$, take the subsequence of values $\sigma(i)$ with $\kappa_i=c$, in increasing order of their positions $i$. If its values are not $1,\ldots,m$ in that order, replace them by their increasing ranks before applying ordinary row insertion. The insertion and reverse-deletion routes use only comparisons, so this order-preserving relabelling leaves every bumping position unchanged; after reverse deletion, replace ranks by the original values in the same order. Thus [F1] gives standard insertion and recording tableaux of the same shape for every color subsequence, including an arbitrary subset of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. At the step for position $i$, record $i$ in the new box of $Q^{(c)}$. Their entries across components are the values $1,\ldots,n$ once in $P$, and the positions $1,\ldots,n$ once in $Q$, so $P,Q$ are standard multitableaux of the same multipartition. This is the stated forward map. [F1, F2]
source_lines.42: 1.2 To invert, begin with standard multitableaux $(P,Q)$ of common shape. At global step $i=n,n-1,\ldots,1$, there is exactly one component $c$ with recording entry $i$. Since every recording component is standard and all larger global labels have already been removed, $i$ is the largest entry in the current $Q^{(c)}$ and occupies a removable corner. Remove that box from $Q^{(c)}$. In $P^{(c)}$, replace the current set of distinct values by their increasing ranks, reverse-row-delete the same corner, and replace the expelled rank by the corresponding original value; this works because both bumping and reverse deletion use only comparisons. Define that value to be $\sigma(i)$ and set $\kappa_i=c$. The process is defined at every step and ends with empty tableaux. [F1, F2]

source_lines.45: 2.1 Relative to the base vertex $[\mathcal O^2]$, a vertex with normalized elementary divisors $(0,n)$ has a chain of length $n$ through $\mathcal O f_1+\pi^j\mathcal O f_2$. If $n>0$, exactly one of its four neighbors has distance parameter $n-1$: in the basis $f_1,\pi^n f_2$ of its representative, the line spanned by $\pi^n f_2$ has inverse image $\pi\mathcal O f_1+\pi^n\mathcal O f_2$, whose homothety class normalizes to parameter $n-1$. Every other line has inverse image with a primitive vector $f_1+t\pi^n f_2$ and second elementary divisor $n+1$, hence parameter $n+1$. At $n=0$ all neighbors have parameter $1$. Therefore the parameter changes by one at each step, and the displayed chain is a shortest path. A cycle would have a vertex of maximal parameter and two distinct adjacent vertices of parameter one less, contradicting uniqueness of the decreasing neighbor. Thus the graph is connected and has no cycle. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]
source_lines.49: 3.1 The unique shortest edge gallery from $E$ to any other edge changes endpoint types alternately: changing twice at the same endpoint would shorten it. In the basis $e_1,\pi^n e_2$, the backward edge corresponds to the line spanned by the second basis vector; the other lines are spanned by $e_1+t\pi^n e_2$ for $t\in\mathbb F_3$, and the displayed matrices send $t$ to $t+b$. For the other initial direction the apartment chain is $L_1,L_0,L_{-1},\ldots,L_{-n}$; use instead $\begin{pmatrix}1&\pi^n b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ at $L_{-n}$, which fixes that earlier chain and is transitive on the three forward lines there. Inductively move each gallery onto the corresponding apartment segment while fixing its earlier segment. Hence $I$ is transitive on the edges with each alternating type word. There are three choices at each extension, so the orbit size is $3^n$. Different words have different type sequences or distances and cannot be in the same orbit. By step 2.2 edges identify with $G/I$, so these orbits are exactly the double cosets. [F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

source_lines.30: These are equalities for the two matrix-algebra images. If $N<n$, no faithfulness of the abstract Hecke algebra is asserted. If $N\ge n$, the abstract Hecke action is faithful. The theorem is only over the rational function field $\mathbb Q(q)$ and asserts no equality at a root of unity, at an arbitrary specialized parameter, or over a field of positive characteristic.
